results.notes: Widely circulated as Ramana Maharshi's response to the question 'How should we treat others?' — a dialogic form consistent with his recorded teachings. Multiple blogs and Quora threads repeat it, but no primary text (e.g., 'Talks with Ramana Maharshi', 'The Collected Works') has been pinpointed as the source. The phrasing is terse and aphoristic in Ramana's style, and the nondual content is entirely consistent with his Advaita Vedanta position. However, because no specific sitting, date, or recorded transcript has been confirmed, this cannot be elevated beyond attributed_unverified. Confidence remains low-to-moderate.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Messenger" (poem), in Thirst, Mary Oliver, Beacon Press, 2006
results.notes: This is the opening line of Mary Oliver's poem 'The Messenger,' the first poem in her collection 'Thirst' (Beacon Press, 2006). Multiple independent literary sources confirm the text and source, including references on Awakin.org, poetry blogs quoting the full poem, and the Beacon Press publication record. The attribution and source are unambiguous. No misattribution concern detected.

Universally attributed to Dōgen Zenji across quote databases (AZQuotes, Goodreads, etc.), but no specific chapter or fascicle of the Shobogenzo has been confirmed as the source in any search result found. The more literal and widely cited Dōgen translation is 'To let the self be awakened by all things is enlightenment' (appearing in multiple Shobogenzo editions). 'Enlightenment is intimacy with all things' reads as an interpretive paraphrase or secondary synthesis rather than a direct translation. The Shobogenzo (1231–1253) is the canonical primary source for Dōgen, but this exact phrasing cannot be pinned to a specific fascicle without further scholarly verification. Plausible but unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: I Am That: Talks with Sri Nisargadatta Maharaj, compiled by Maurice Frydman, 1973
results.notes: Wikiquote's Nisargadatta Maharaj article contains the fuller passage: 'Love says I am everything. Wisdom says I am nothing. Between the two, my life flows.' This is cited to 'I Am That,' the landmark compilation of his dialogues by Maurice Frydman (1973). The quote as given in our record ('Love tells me I am everything. Wisdom tells me I am nothing. And between the two my life flows.') is a minor paraphrase of the same passage. Also cited by Sharon Salzberg in 'Lovingkindness.' The author name 'Swami Nisargadatta' is non-standard; he is canonically known as 'Sri Nisargadatta Maharaj.' Attribution is strongly supported by Wikiquote and multiple secondary references, though exact page number in 'I Am That' was not located in web results.

results.earliest_print_source: "My Rose Petals," Sri Chinmoy, Sri Chinmoy Centre, 1971 (earliest confirmed print version)
results.notes: This quote is almost certainly not original to Jimi Hendrix. Goodreads tags it explicitly as 'misattributed' and cross-references 'william-gladstone.' Wikiquote's Sri Chinmoy article contains the note that 'a similar statement has also become attributed to Jimi Hendrix, though he could have been quoting or paraphrasing Chinmoy, or conceivably Gladstone.' Sri Chinmoy's 'My Rose Petals' (1971) is the earliest confirmed print citation: 'World Peace can be achieved when the Power Of Love replaces the Love Of Power.' William Gladstone is cited in 'The Forbes Book of Business Quotations' (1997) and in 'The National Elementary School Principal' (Vol. 28, 1948) with a very similar phrasing. An even earlier origin attributed to William Ellery Channing (1780–1842) circulates but is unverified. The exact phrasing in this record ('becomes stronger than' rather than 'overcomes') is a further variant. No primary Hendrix source (interview, recording, written statement) has ever been established. Misattribution to Hendrix is well-documented.
results.suggested_reattribution: Sri Chinmoy (earliest confirmed print, 1971); possibly William Gladstone or William Ellery Channing for an earlier conceptual antecedent

results.notes: Consistently and widely attributed to Thich Nhat Hanh across Buddhist and mindfulness publications (HuffPost, Pachamama Alliance, Mountain Sangha, etc.). One secondary source (mountainsangha.org) specifically states the quote appeared in a Tricycle.com article by dharma teacher Wendy Johnson, citing it as Thich Nhat Hanh's words. However, no specific book or talk by Thich Nhat Hanh has been pinpointed in any search result. Given the broad and consistent attribution, including from organizations closely aligned with his teaching lineage, confidence is moderate-to-high. Cannot be elevated to 'verified' without a specific primary text reference.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Crack-Up," F. Scott Fitzgerald, Esquire magazine, February 1936
results.notes: Confirmed by Quote Investigator (quoteinvestigator.com/2020/01/05/intelligence/), which identified the original text in Fitzgerald's autobiographical essay 'The Crack-Up,' first published in Esquire in February 1936 and later collected in the posthumous book of the same name (New Directions, 1945). QI concludes: 'F. Scott Fitzgerald should receive credit for the statement he wrote in 1936.' PBS's American Masters page and the essay text itself corroborate this. The quote as given is very close to the original; the original uses 'in the mind' rather than 'in mind,' a negligible variant. No misattribution concern.

Quote Investigator (quoteinvestigator.com/2020/05/13/make-friends/) investigated this thoroughly and concluded: 'based on current evidence this anecdote is apocryphal.' The saying has been attributed to Abraham Lincoln (via a post-mortem Civil War anecdote), Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund (d. 1437), and Mark Twain — all attributions appearing long after each figure's death. An 1867 New Orleans newspaper attributed a similar saying to Sigismund; the Lincoln anecdote form emerged by the 1940s. An 1858 Wisconsin newspaper cited the concept in relation to Cardinal Richelieu. An 1885 Vermont newspaper printed a similar line with no attribution. No primary Lincoln source (speech, letter, diary) has ever been found. The attribution to Lincoln is not credible.

results.earliest_print_source: The Wisdom of Insecurity: A Message for an Age of Anxiety, Alan Watts, Pantheon Books, 1951
results.notes: Multiple independent sources (libquotes.com, AZQuotes, buboquote, wist.info) consistently cite this quote to Alan Watts's 'The Wisdom of Insecurity: A Message for an Age of Anxiety' (Pantheon Books, 1951). One source (wist.info) references a specific chapter. The attribution is stable across all major quote databases and is never disputed. Cannot be elevated to 'verified' (1.0) without a page-confirmed primary text check, but the evidence is strong and consistent. No misattribution concern.

The official Ram Dass Foundation website (ramdass.org/ram-dass-quotes/) carries this quote, lending it institutional credibility. Goodreads also has the extended version: 'The most important aspect of love is not in giving or the receiving: it's in the being. When I need love from others, or need to give love to others, I'm caught in an unstable situation.' Note the official source uses 'the receiving' not merely 'receiving' as in this record — a minor wording variant. No specific book title (e.g., 'Be Here Now,' 'Grist for the Mill,' 'How Can I Help?') has been identified as the origin in any source found. Attribution is plausible and officially endorsed, but the absence of a traceable book source keeps confidence at the moderate level.

"God in drag" is a documented Ram Dass idiom — he used it repeatedly in lectures and it is consistently attributed to him across his own foundation's materials and secondary collections. The usual circulated phrasing is "Treat everyone you meet like God in drag." I cannot place it in a specific book or dated talk from my own knowledge, so this is strong-secondary rather than primary. No fabricated citation offered.

Consistent with Ram Dass's vocabulary ("unfolding," "opportunities to awaken") and circulates attributed to him, but I know of no talk, book, or dated interview that fixes it. Plausible but unverified.

Reads as an excerpt lifted from a longer Ram Dass passage about loving from the soul plane rather than the ego plane — a theme he taught constantly — but as a standalone sentence it is not one of his widely circulated lines and I cannot locate a source. The fragmentary phrasing suggests it may be a transcription of spoken remarks, possibly out of context.

results.earliest_print_source: Commencement Address, Stanford University, Steve Jobs, 12 June 2005
results.notes: Genuine and primary-sourced. Delivered in the second story ("love and loss") of the Stanford commencement address, 12 June 2005; the full sentence continues "...And the only way to do great work is to love what you do. If you haven't found it yet, keep looking. Don't settle." Transcript and video are published by Stanford.

results.earliest_print_source: Apple "Think Different" advertising campaign copy, TBWA\Chiat\Day, 1997
results.notes: This is the closing line of the Apple "Think Different" ad copy (1997), not a Jobs original. The copy was written at TBWA\Chiat\Day; creative director Rob Siltanen has publicly claimed principal authorship (with Lee Clow and Craig Tanimoto involved), and Jobs's role was as client, editor, and narrator of the unaired version he recorded. Because Jobs voiced it, it is universally credited to him. The ad wording is "the ones who are crazy enough to think they can change the world, are the ones who do" — the quoted text inserts "that." Attribution to Jobs as author is weak; my confidence in the ad-copy origin is high, but the individual copywriter credit is contested, so the reattribution below names the campaign rather than one person.
results.suggested_reattribution: Apple "Think Different" campaign copy (TBWA\Chiat\Day — Rob Siltanen, Lee Clow, Craig Tanimoto), 1997

results.earliest_print_source: Commencement Address, Stanford University, Steve Jobs, 12 June 2005
results.notes: Confirms the pre-flag: genuine, from the third story ("death") of the 2005 Stanford commencement address. Wording matches the published transcript with two small copy issues to fix before use: "the noise of other's opinions" should be "others' opinions," and the dash in "dogma - which is" should be an em dash. Otherwise verbatim.

results.earliest_print_source: "Old Man's Advice to Youth: 'Never Lose a Holy Curiosity,'" LIFE magazine, 2 May 1955, p. 64
results.notes: A rare case where an Einstein quotation of this kind is genuine. It comes from remarks Einstein made to William Miller, published in LIFE shortly after Einstein's death in April 1955 under the headline that itself quotes the last line. This is one of the sourced entries on Einstein's Wikiquote page rather than one of the many unsourced accretions. Wording as given matches the published version.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book 12 (Gregory Hays translation, Modern Library, 2002)
results.notes: Genuine Marcus Aurelius, but note this is specifically Gregory Hays's 2002 English rendering — the colloquial "dance like a puppet" is Hays's phrasing, not a literal or older translation, so the wording is translator-dependent and other translations read quite differently. I place it in Book 12, most likely section 19, though I am working from memory on the exact section number and have not confirmed it. Translator credit should be carried with the quote.

Genuine Chomsky in substance and voice; it is the opening of a longer passage that continues roughly "If you assume that there is no hope, you guarantee that there will be no hope. If you assume that there is an instinct for freedom, that there are opportunities to change things, then there is a possibility that you can contribute to making a better world." That longer form circulates widely and consistently under his name from interviews. I cannot fix the specific interview, date, or volume, so I have left the source null rather than guess at one of the several collections it is often credited to.

results.earliest_print_source: The Story of Philosophy, Will Durant, Simon & Schuster, 1926
results.notes: The pre-flag is correct and this is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The sentence is Will Durant's own summarizing gloss on the Nicomachean Ethics (roughly 1103a-b, on virtue as hexis acquired by habituation), written in The Story of Philosophy (1926). Aristotle never wrote it; Durant's line is set immediately after his paraphrase of Aristotle and the quotation marks migrated over time. Wikiquote lists it under Aristotle's misattributed section. Recommend crediting Durant and, if the Aristotelian idea is wanted, citing Nicomachean Ethics directly instead.
results.suggested_reattribution: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), paraphrasing Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics

results.earliest_print_source: John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan," Saturday Review, 18 March 1967
results.notes: The attribution as recorded in this record is already correct, which is unusual and worth preserving. Culkin wrote "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us" while summarizing McLuhan's argument; McLuhan himself did not write the sentence in this form. Two cautions: (a) the corpus text "thereafter our tools shape us" is a later smoothing of Culkin's wording — consider restoring the original; (b) the line is often confused with Churchill's "We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us" (House of Commons, 28 October 1943), which is a genuinely separate quotation and a likely source of the "thereafter" construction.

results.earliest_print_source: Psychological Types, C. G. Jung, 1921 (Collected Works vol. 6, para. 197)
results.notes: Genuine Jung, from the discussion of Schiller in Psychological Types. The full sentence continues "...but by the play instinct acting from inner necessity. The creative mind plays with the objects it loves." The corpus text truncates "acting from inner necessity," which changes the emphasis somewhat — restoring the full sentence would be more faithful. Paragraph number 197 is from memory and should be spot-checked against a print copy of CW 6.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Maslow, and entirely consistent with his writing on creativeness in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) and The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971), where he discusses spontaneity and play in primary creativity. But I cannot place this exact eight-word sentence in either book or in any paper, and short aphoristic sentences of this shape are frequently condensations made by later writers rather than the author's own line. Honest verdict: probably Maslow-derived, source unconfirmed.

I associate this line with David Lynch's Inland Empire (2006), where it is spoken as dialogue and continues "...But who is the dreamer?" Lynch also used the formulation in talks about consciousness and Transcendental Meditation, and has framed it as echoing an Upanishadic idea rather than as his own invention — so "Lynch" is right as the popularizer but may not be right as the originator. I am confident enough in the Lynch connection to call this attributed, but not confident enough in the film citation to record it as a source, so the field is left null.

Squarely in Tolle's idiom and theme — The Power of Now and A New Earth both argue for unconditional acceptance of the present moment ("Always say yes to the present moment"; "Whatever the present moment contains, accept it as if you had chosen it"). But I cannot match this specific four-sentence sequence to a passage in either book, and Tolle quotations circulating on social media are frequently paraphrases assembled from his talks. Plausibly genuine, unsourced.

One of the most-quoted lines in innovation and design circles, and consistent with Fuller's actual programme of "comprehensive anticipatory design science" and his stated preference for artifacts over reform. However, to my knowledge it sits in the unsourced/attributed section of Fuller's Wikiquote page rather than being traced to Critical Path, Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, or any dated lecture, and the crisp two-sentence form has the shape of a later condensation. I am not willing to name a book I cannot confirm. Genuinely Fuller-ish; provenance open.

I cannot place this line in Arthur Miller's plays, essays, or the autobiography Timebends (1987). It has the cadence of a line from After the Fall (1964), which is preoccupied with seeing oneself and others truthfully, but that is a guess and I will not record it as a source. Low confidence in the attribution; also worth checking whether the Arthur Miller intended is the playwright at all, since the name is common.

Consistently attributed to Nisargadatta Maharaj and almost certainly from I Am That (dialogues recorded 1970-73, translated by Maurice Frydman, first published 1973), which is the source of nearly all his circulating aphorisms. I have not confirmed the chapter or page, so the source field is left null rather than half-cited. Data fix required: the author name is misspelled in the record — "Nisagardatta" should be "Nisargadatta Maharaj" (commonly "Sri Nisargadatta Maharaj"). Also note the text uses an en dash where most printings have a comma or semicolon.

Consistently attributed to Lennon and strongly associated with the run of interviews he gave in September-December 1980 (the David Sheff Playboy interview, the Newsweek and RKO sessions) in which he repeatedly defended the sincerity of the 1960s peace message against the charge that it was naive or dated. The content and register fit those interviews well. I cannot confirm which interview, so no source is recorded.

results.earliest_print_source: Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times: A Book of Meditations, David Viscott, Contemporary Books, 1993
results.notes: No evidence Picasso ever said or wrote this, and it does not appear in his documented statements on art. The traceable origin is psychiatrist and broadcaster David Viscott, whose 1993 meditation book contains the line in the form "The purpose of life is to discover your gift. The meaning of life is to give your gift away." Note that the popular Picasso version swaps "meaning" and "purpose" relative to Viscott's original — a signature of a quote that has been passed along orally rather than copied from a text. Attribution to Picasso should be treated as false.
results.suggested_reattribution: David Viscott, Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times (1993)

results.earliest_print_source: Strength to Love, Martin Luther King Jr., Harper & Row, 1963 (sermon "Loving Your Enemies")
results.notes: Genuine King, from the "Loving Your Enemies" sermon, preached at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in the late 1950s and published in Strength to Love (1963). Small wording fix: the published line reads "transforming an enemy into a friend" — the corpus text drops the article "a." Recommend restoring it.

results.earliest_print_source: Strength to Love, Martin Luther King Jr., Harper & Row, 1963 (sermon "Our God Is Able")
results.notes: Genuine King and characteristic of his personalist theology — "cosmic companionship" is a phrase he used in several sermons and in the Nobel lecture context. I place this passage in "Our God Is Able" in Strength to Love, though I am identifying the specific sermon from memory rather than from a checked text, which is why this is attributed rather than verified. Wording note: King's published phrasing is "Behind the harsh appearances of the world" (plural), and the passage is normally one continuous sentence rather than the two the corpus text splits it into.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Grand Miracle," C. S. Lewis, The Guardian, 27 April 1945; collected in God in the Dock (1970)
results.notes: Genuine Lewis, from the essay "The Grand Miracle," first published in the Anglican weekly The Guardian in 1945 and later collected in God in the Dock (ed. Walter Hooper, 1970). The idea also appears in his book Miracles (1947), which is why the quote is sometimes credited there instead; the essay is the earlier appearance. Wording as given matches my recollection of the published text.

Consistent in doctrine and translation register with the recorded sayings of Sri Anandamayi Ma (1896-1982) as published in the Matri Vani volumes and similar compilations issued by her ashram — the capitalized "Beloved" and the formal English are typical of those translations. I cannot identify which volume or which recorded conversation, and the compilations are themselves edited transcriptions of Bengali speech, so even a located citation would be a translation of a translation. Honest verdict: plausibly authentic, unsourced.

Same assessment as q_0044: the diction, the emphasis on constant remembrance and repetition of the Name, and the closing turn to realization of the Self all fit the published English renderings of Sri Anandamayi Ma's sayings (the Matri Vani / Sad Vani family of ashram compilations), but I cannot identify the volume. IMPORTANT DATA DEFECTS, likely OCR damage, that must be fixed before this text is used anywhere: "for the man who has found film" should read "found Him"; the word rendered "Him-self" contains an embedded soft hyphen (U+00AD) that should be stripped. The passage is also long enough that it may be a stitched-together excerpt rather than one continuous saying — worth checking against a print source before promotion.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Theo van Gogh, Arles, September 1888 (collected in The Complete Letters of Vincent van Gogh)
results.notes: This is a genuine line from Van Gogh's correspondence with his brother Theo, from a letter written at Arles in September 1888. Translations vary between 'nothing more truly artistic' and 'nothing more genuinely artistic than to love people', which is the usual signature of a real translated letter rather than an invented aphorism. I am confident of the letter's existence and rough date but cannot recall the catalogue letter number from memory, so I have not asserted one.

Circulates consistently under Haile Selassie's name and the register matches his many public addresses on education and pan-African cooperation ('great common achievements' is his diction). The likely home is one of the speeches gathered in the official Selected Speeches of His Imperial Majesty Haile Selassie I, but I cannot place the specific address or date from memory, so I have not asserted a citation. Attribution is plausible but unverified.

This is a Daniel Ladinsky line, not Hafez. Ladinsky's popular 'Hafiz' volumes (The Gift; I Heard God Laughing) are his own original poems, not translations — he has said in his own prefaces that they came to him rather than from the Persian text, and scholars of Persian literature (and Wikiquote's Hafez page) treat the whole Ladinsky corpus as unattributable to Hafez. This aphorism's compressed, modern-English epigram form is unlike any authentic ghazal line. I did not attempt to name which Ladinsky volume it appears in, since I am not certain.

Doctrinally and verbally characteristic of Ram Dass's later teaching — the detachment/devotion pairing is a theme he returned to often — and it circulates through the Love Serve Remember Foundation's channels, which are a reasonably careful custodian of his words. But most such lines come from unindexed recorded talks, and I cannot place this one in any of his books. Attribution plausible, source untraced.

Consistent with Ram Dass's teaching on love and fear (a recurring theme in his later work, including Polishing the Mirror and Walking Each Other Home), and widely circulated under his name. I cannot locate it in a specific book or dated talk, so the attribution stands unverified.

A short aphorism circulated under Ram Dass's name, mostly through social media and quote aggregators. The sentiment fits him, but the line is generic enough that it could equally be a paraphrase of him or someone else's phrasing that drifted onto his name. No traceable source in my knowledge; lower confidence than the other Ram Dass lines in this batch because there is nothing distinctive to anchor it.

The best-anchored of the Ram Dass lines in this batch. 'Suffering only shows you where you are attached' is a formula he used repeatedly in talks and is frequently quoted from the Grist for the Mill era; the 'suffering is grace' close is also his. Attribution is very likely correct, but I cannot cite a specific book page or dated recording, so it stays below the verified/attributed evidentiary bar.

results.earliest_print_source: The World According to Mister Rogers: Important Things to Remember, Fred Rogers, 2003
results.notes: Genuine Fred Rogers. The 'active noun like struggle' formulation is distinctive and is consistently attributed to him; it appears in the authorized posthumous collection The World According to Mister Rogers (2003). Rogers used the line earlier in his own writings and talks, so 2003 is where it appears in print rather than necessarily its first utterance. Common variant ends 'right here and now' rather than 'here and now'.

Attributed to Elie Wiesel in quote collections and memorial pieces, but I cannot place it in Night or in any of his other books, essays, or Nobel-related addresses that I know. It is short and generic enough to have drifted onto his name from a paraphrase of his testimony about the camps. Honest answer: unverified.

Pete Holmes is a living comedian whose quotable material comes mainly from the You Made It Weird podcast and his memoir Comedy Sex God (2019); this line reads exactly like his podcast register and is circulated under his name. But podcast talk is effectively uncitable without the episode, and I cannot confirm whether he originated it or was relaying someone else's formulation — he often credits others mid-conversation. Plausible, untraced.

One of the most widely circulated Watts lines, and the work/play inversion is a genuine and central Watts theme rather than an internet invention. It almost certainly comes from one of his recorded lectures, which is why no book citation attaches to it. Attribution is consistent across sources but I can offer no primary, and some Watts compilations carry it in their unsourced sections. Usual wording is 'what you are doing in the here and now'; the record drops 'in the here and'.

The idea (that life has no destination beyond the present moment) is thoroughly Watts, but this exact compressed sentence I cannot place in his books or in the lecture material I know. Short aphorisms in this shape are frequently distilled by others out of longer Watts passages and then quoted as if verbatim. Treat the wording as unverified even though the thought is his.

Strongly suspect. The vocabulary is wrong for Watts: 'degree of productivity' and 'presence' as a self-help metric belong to 2010s wellness writing, not to a mid-century writer whose target was the Protestant work ethic in quite different terms. I know of no occurrence in his published work, and this reads like an internet aphorism given a Watts byline for authority. I cannot name the actual author, so I have not proposed a reattribution — but I would not promote this as Watts.

Sounds authentically Watts and fits the argument of The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951), which is his sustained treatment of anxiety — that is the likeliest home for it. I am not confident enough of the page or even the book to assert the citation, and it may equally come from a lecture. Consistently attributed, source untraced.

This formulation is classically Meister Eckhart's ('the soul is not in the body; the body is in the soul'), and the underlying doctrine is Plotinian — the Enneads argue expressly that the body is in the soul rather than the soul in the body. Watts read and quoted Eckhart constantly, so he may well have said this in a lecture, but he would have been relaying it, not coining it. Attributing it to Watts as author is likely wrong. My confidence in Eckhart as the formulator is moderate rather than high, hence the hedge.

Genuine Thich Nhat Hanh in substance and voice — attention as the most precious gift, and the blooming-flower image for those we attend to, are both signature formulations he used across many books and talks. The pairing appears in his Parallax Press volumes (How to Love is the collection most often cited for it), but he reworked these lines repeatedly and I cannot fix a first appearance, so I have left the print source null rather than guess a book.

Gandhi is a misattribution magnet, so I weighted this cautiously. Unlike most 'Gandhi' internet quotes, this one has a long and stable pre-internet circulation with consistent wording and is generally accepted as his, plausibly from a 1930s speech or writing collected in the Collected Works. But I cannot place it in a specific text or date, and I cannot rule out that it is a paraphrase tightened by a later editor. Attribution likely correct; evidence short of the promotion bar.

The record's author field is 'Anonymous', which is defensible but incomplete: this passage circulates very widely as Bhagavad Gita, and the record's own context tag ('Hindu, Krishna-consciousness') points the same way. It is not a literal translation of any verse I can identify — it reads as a loose devotional paraphrase in the manner of popular English Gita anthologies rather than of Sanskrit rendered line by line. So 'Bhagavad Gita' would be the conventional attribution, but a real verse anchor is exactly what I cannot supply.
results.suggested_reattribution: Bhagavad Gita (conventional attribution; appears to be a loose paraphrase, not a verse translation)

results.notes: A signature Rod McKuen line, quoted as his in profiles and in obituary coverage after his death in 2015, which is decent independent evidence that it predates internet quote culture. His enormous 1960s-70s output (Listen to the Warm, Stanyan Street & Other Sorrows, and the spoken-word records) is the likely home, but I cannot name the poem or album, so no citation asserted. Data note: the author field is 'Rod McKuen,' with a trailing comma and should be cleaned.

Consistently and, as far as I know, uncontestedly attributed to Alice Walker; I am aware of no competing claimant or misattribution history, which is the main risk this check screens for. The likely origin is an interview or essay rather than her fiction, and I cannot name it, so the confidence reflects a solid attribution with no primary in hand.

Attributed to Lloyd George in twentieth-century quotation dictionaries and business-motivation collections with reasonable consistency, so it is not a recent invention. But I know of no speech, letter, or memoir passage where he says it, and aphorisms of this shape are routinely assigned to convenient statesmen. Plausible, unverified; I would not promote it without a primary.

results.earliest_print_source: The Journal of Henry David Thoreau, entry of 25 July 1839
results.notes: Genuine Thoreau, from an early Journal entry of 1839 (the date is conventionally given as 25 July; I am confident of the Journal and the year, slightly less of the exact day). Quoted verbatim here, with no drift in the wording.

results.earliest_print_source: The Journal of Henry David Thoreau, entry of April 1841
results.notes: Genuine Thoreau, from a Journal entry of spring 1841 (usually dated 5 April 1841). The passage is quoted accurately, including the 'island of opportunities' image, which is the distinctive part and the reason I can place it with confidence. I am sure of the Journal and the year; the exact day is the conventional citation rather than something I can independently confirm.

results.earliest_print_source: The Journal of Henry David Thoreau (entry conventionally dated 26 January 1853)
results.notes: Genuine Thoreau in substance, and the source is his Journal rather than Walden, which is where popular reprints often place it. Thoreau's own wording is tighter — 'Many go a-fishing all their lives without knowing that it is not fish they are after' — so the record's 'Many men go fishing all of their lives' is a smoothed later version. I am confident of the Journal attribution and less so of the exact date, which I give as the conventional one. Data note: the text begins with a stray invisible character (U+200E) before 'Many' and should be cleaned.

results.earliest_print_source: Walden, Henry David Thoreau, 1854 ('Conclusion') — paraphrased
results.notes: The author is right but the wording is not Thoreau's. Walden's Conclusion reads: 'I learned this, at least, by my experiment: that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavours to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.' The two-sentence imperative version is a twentieth-century condensation that circulates on posters and graduation cards. Held below the promotion bar deliberately: the attribution is sound, but the text as recorded should be corrected to the Walden passage or explicitly marked as a paraphrase before it goes live.
